extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of science, scientists, and students of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and tests for evaluating causal claims and scientific explanations: what counts as a cause, how to distinguish real causation from mere concomitance, limits of generalization, and the evidential burden for positing efficient (including volitional or divine) causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Causation: change can only be produced by change
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of causation is that change can only be produced by change; along with any number of stationary antecedents (collocations) there must be at least one changing antecedent (a force).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying causes, ensure there is an active (changing) antecedent in addition to the necessary arrangement or collocation of objects. Examples: a bonfire requires not only fuel, air, and spark (collocations) but chemical action (a force); grinding corn requires correct collocation of mill parts and a moving force such as flowing water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause comprises both a force and a collocation (Bain's distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the assemblage of conditions that constitutes the cause of a phenomenon, distinguish two elements: (1) the presence of a force; and (2) the collocation or position of objects required for the force to undergo the particular transmutation that constitutes the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate collocation (arrangement of parts) with active force; the collocation, as commonly conceived, may include the property that gives force, but analytical clarity requires separating the two when explaining sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vera causa requirement for legitimate hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses invoked to explain phenomena should posit a vera causa — a true/legitimate cause — rather than mere fanciful mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of inventing auxiliary entities (e.g., a subtle ether penetrating all bodies) solely to save a theory; the proposed cause should be credible as a real causal agent. The text illustrates that some suppositions (like an all-pervading ether) are hypotheses made for explanatory convenience and should be scrutinized for legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept potential properties (potentiality of motion) as antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Force should be conceived as potentiality of motion rather than necessarily actual motion; antecedent may be a property of objects (fit to be the antecedent of an effect) rather than active motion at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accounting for effects (e.g., heat from coal, motion of a stone from a height), recognize that the causal antecedent can be a stored or potential property. This allows maintaining causal accounts without requiring continuous prior actual motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expenditure or transfer of energy as a test to distinguish causation from mere concomitance
rubrics_metrics.description: One practical test for distinguishing causation from concomitance is the expenditure or transfer of energy: if the effect involves putting matter into motion, then any object present that has lost motion has contributed to the effect and may be the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use energetic accounting where applicable: identify which antecedent(s) have supplied or lost motion/energy corresponding to the effect. This helps select among antecedents the one that exerts active force and so is the true cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require positive external evidence before positing volition (will) as an efficient cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that Will (volition) is the only or primary efficient cause of phenomena rests on an alleged direct consciousness of causal power; such subjective feeling is not positive external evidence that volition is an efficient cause beyond cases of nervous/muscular action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept volition as an efficient cause of external phenomena merely because we feel effort in willing. The analogies with paralysis and the need for experience show consciousness of volition does not provide a priori knowledge of its efficacy; positive empirical evidence is needed before generalizing volition as an efficient cause of non-mental phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base theory choice solely on conceivability or subjective 'naturalness'
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorists who prefer one causal account over another often rely on which sequence appears more 'natural' or 'conceivable' to them; this is a subjective criterion tied to individual experience and habit, not a universal law for choosing between theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer external empirical evidence and objective tests over appeals to conceivability. Recognize that what appears intelligible or natural varies by upbringing, discipline, and familiarity; conceivability alone cannot decide between competing causal hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalize only from instances that closely resemble the known case
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalization from a single known instance to others is justified only when the other instances resemble the known one in relevant respects (i.e., manifest the same sorts of indications and conform to the same laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sweeping inferences (e.g., because volition causes our bodily motions therefore it causes all natural phenomena; or because our world is inhabited therefore every heavenly body is inhabited). Require demonstrable similarity (shared laws, shared manifestations) before extending causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use linguistic and historical evidence cautiously to infer past beliefs and instinctive philosophies
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure and vocabulary of languages, and historical accounts, can indicate early human tendencies to attribute agency to natural objects (e.g., active verbs applied to sun, moon, winds), revealing an instinctive 'volitional' explanation of phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing historical or psychological origins of causal beliefs, consider linguistic structures as useful evidence of prevalent early conceptions, but corroborate with other historical sources; language shows tendencies but is not an infallible record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not invoke supernatural or divine efficient causes merely from inability to conceive mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking God or divine will as the efficient cause (occasionalism) because material mechanisms seem inconceivable is a methodological fallacy: inability to conceive a natural connection does not justify positing supernatural agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist the temptation to fill explanatory gaps with divine agency simply because the mechanism is presently obscure; instead, treat such invocations as a failure to supply empirical causal accounts and seek further inquiry into possible physical antecedents.
